subject: dropping correlated variables OR shrinkage parameter? which one as solution to multi-collinearity?

messages.author: 1d32e0a5b2a0b684
messages.subject: dropping correlated variables OR shrinkage parameter? which one as solution to multi-collinearity?
parts:
Hi everyone,

I will be grateful for any advice/suggestion/help:

My original data suffers from multicollinearity, with several variables highly-correlated at r > .9

So I get several warning messages from lavaan, sem function; I only know two ways to deal with this issue: either dropping highly-correlated variables from the model or using a shrinkage parameter (e.g., regularization).

I tried both; with former one the model doesn't fit. with the latter one, I used the corpcor package to apply shrinkage parameter (it's L2 regularization method, you can check here) with the cov.shrink() function; I don't know if I should apply this shrinkage to the original raw data as a metrix or should I apply it to the covariance matrix? Any one could help? I think the actual covariance matrix (without shrinkage) is non-positive definite because determinant is 3.362909e-42


when I use it with original data matrix, I get below warning messages; I write the code and error messages below:

library(lavaan)
library(corpcor)

data <- matrix(data)
cov.shrink<- cov.shrink(data)

is.positive.definite(cov.shrink)
TRUE

fit<- sem(model, sample.cov = cov.shrink, sample.nobs=210)

Warning messages:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
2: In lavaan::lavaan(model = lex.model2F, sample.cov = cov.shrink.lexdata,  :
  lavaan WARNING: not all elements of the gradient are (near) zero;
                  the optimizer may not have found a local solution;
                  use lavInspect(fit, "optim.gradient") to investigate


---even when I add the argument ridge = .01 to the sem function it gives the same error and terrible fit indices:

fit<- sem(model, sample.cov = cov.shrink, sample.nobs=210, ridge = .01)


----Am I allowed to once apply shrinkage to the data, then again use the ridge option in the sem function as above??
--Any better way of dealing with this issue?

Many thanks,
maryam

messages.subject: Re: dropping correlated variables OR shrinkage parameter? which one as solution to multi-collinearity?
parts: Am I allowed to once apply shrinkage to the data, then again use the ridge option in the sem function as above?
Any better way of dealing with this issue?

These aren't really lavaan questions.  SEMNET has a broader audience of SEM experts, and it is a more general forum:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

It will help to describe your actual model and the goal of the analysis when asking advice.  My first thought is that you should use the lasso to select among redundant predictors before you try doing anything in SEM.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: dropping correlated variables OR shrinkage parameter? which one as solution to multi-collinearity?
parts:
Thanks Terrence for your helpful advice. I will try lasso as well.

I have already posted on SEMNET, it seems both sides of the argument have their own logical and statistical evidence to favour either shrinkage parameter or dropping variables. I tried both but the model still does not fit. Someone also suggested not dropping variables and not using regularisation, just change the model. This also doesnt seem to work.

I was wondering of there is any other type of tests (e.g., machine learning method, etc) that doent have assumptions of normality and collinearity and just find the underlying structure of the data and the grouping of variables which measure the same underlying construct.

Or should I take the misfit as a genuine model misfit and go forward with EFA to find a better model and then test that again with CFA/SEM?

Thanks 
Maryam
